questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why water molecules attract each other
questions.stem: A nurse hands over a note stating water molecules attract each other because of partial charges; which property explains this?

options.text: Water molecules have a bent shape creating partial positive and negative ends
Water molecules share electrons equally between hydrogen and oxygen atoms
options.misconception: assumes electrons are shared equally in water

options.text: Water molecules form ionic bonds that lock atoms into a rigid lattice
options.misconception: confuses polar covalent bonds with ionic bonds

options.text: Water molecules are nonpolar so they mix freely with oils and fats
options.misconception: treats water as nonpolar and miscible with oils

questions.explanation: Water is polar because oxygen pulls electrons more strongly than hydrogen, giving partial charges that attract neighboring molecules. The tempting ionic-bond idea fails because no full electron transfer occurs.
questions.hint: Look for partial charges, not full ionic transfer.

questions.hint: Beading means molecules prefer each other over the surface.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY

questions.stem: A nurse prepares a capillary tube of radius 0.5 mm; given water surface tension 0.0728 N/m and density 1000 kg/m3, what height does water rise in meters? Use g=9.8.

Water molecules are the heaviest among similar molecules
Extensive hydrogen bonding requires much heat to break
Water has a low specific heat so it heats quickly
options.misconception: confuses specific heat with boiling point

questions.explanation: Strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds need substantial energy to break, raising boiling point. The mass idea ignores intermolecular forces.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Apply tetravalence to molecular structure
questions.stem: A nurse handover draws a carbon with five bonds; what is wrong with this structure?

options.text: Five bonds are allowed if one is ionic
Carbon should form only single bonds
Carbon must bond only to hydrogen
Carbon exceeds its four-bond valence

questions.explanation: Carbon forms at most four covalent bonds; five violates tetravalence. The single-bonds-only idea is too restrictive but not the core error.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why carbon skeletons vary widely
questions.stem: A handover note asks why carbon skeletons can be straight, branched, or rings; explain.

answer.exemplar: Carbon's four valence bonds allow each carbon to connect to multiple others in chains, branches, or rings, creating diverse skeletons.

questions.explanation: Four bonds per carbon enable varied connectivity and skeleton shapes. A tempting wrong idea is that different elements create the variety.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Relate bond order to molecular geometry
questions.stem: A handover note includes a molecule with a triple bond; how many atoms are directly bonded by that triple bond?

options.text: Three atoms are bonded together by one triple bond
options.misconception: confuses bond order with atom count

options.text: Two atoms share three pairs of electrons
One atom bonds to three separate atoms
options.misconception: misreads triple bond as three single bonds

options.text: Four atoms form a tetrahedral triple bond

questions.explanation: A triple bond connects two atoms with three shared pairs. The three-atoms idea confuses bond order with connectivity count.
questions.hint: Triple bond is between two atoms.

questions.stem: A nurse handover shows carbon bonded to nitrogen with two hydrogens; which group is present?

An amino group (-NH2) attached to carbon
A thiol group because sulfur is nearby

questions.explanation: Carbon bonded to -NH2 forms an amino group. The hydroxyl idea confuses nitrogen-containing with oxygen-containing groups.

questions.topic: Acids and Bases: Proton Donors and Acceptors
questions.learningObjective: Classify a species as acid or base
questions.stem: A handover note labels HCl in water; by Bronsted-Lowry, HCl acts as what?

options.text: A buffer because it stabilizes pH
A base because it accepts a proton from water
A catalyst because it speeds water dissociation
An acid because it donates a proton to water

questions.explanation: HCl donates a proton to water, acting as a Bronsted-Lowry acid. The base idea reverses the proton transfer direction.

questions.stem: A nurse handover shows a carbon with both C=O and -OH on the same carbon; which group is this?

An ether because oxygen links two carbons

questions.learningObjective: Predict micelle formation
questions.stem: A handover note describes soap in water; what structure forms spontaneously?

Micelles with hydrophobic tails outward and heads inward
A solid precipitate because soap is insoluble
Micelles with hydrophilic heads outward and hydrophobic tails inward

questions.explanation: Amphipathic soap molecules self-assemble into micelles with polar heads facing water. The reversed orientation would expose hydrophobic tails to water.

questions.stem: A handover note places a cell in pure water; what happens to cell volume?

options.text: Cell shrinks as water leaves by osmosis
Cell swells as water enters by osmosis
Cell volume stays unchanged because membrane blocks water

questions.explanation: Pure water is hypotonic relative to cytoplasm, so water enters and cell swells. The shrink idea reverses the gradient.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Water: Preparing a Solution of Known Molarity
questions.learningObjective: Calculate volume needed for a target molarity
questions.stem: A nurse needs 0.25 mol of solute at 0.5 M concentration; what volume in liters is required?
questions.explanation: Volume equals moles divided by molarity: 0.25 divided by 0.5 equals 0.5 L. The tempting error is multiplying moles by molarity.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Acids and Bases: Choosing a Buffer from Data
questions.learningObjective: Justify buffer selection with data
questions.stem: A handover note lists buffers pKa 3.2 and 9.1 for a target pH 7.4; which should be chosen and why?

answer.exemplar: Choose the buffer whose pKa is closest to 7.4; here 9.1 is closer than 3.2, so it provides better buffering near physiological pH.

questions.explanation: Buffer effectiveness peaks near pKa, so the closer pKa to target pH is preferred. A tempting wrong idea is that either buffer works at any pH.
questions.hint: Closer pKa to target is better.
